passage: I'm Rafiq. I sit next to Jahnavi in Class 10, so I saw her history project feedback sheet when Ma'am handed it back. I counted. Nine ticks, with comments like 'excellent map', 'clear timeline', 'lovely use of sources'. And one line at the bottom in red: 'Conclusion is rushed.' She read it for a long time. At lunch she told Anjali, 'Ma'am hated my conclusion.' After school she told her mother on the phone, 'She said my project was rushed.' Not the conclusion. The project. By evening, in our class chat, she wrote: 'history project was a disaster lol.' I don't know exactly what she felt. But I saw the sheet. It wasn't a disaster. It had nine good things and one thing to fix, and somehow only the red line went home with her.

qa.q: What did the red line on Jahnavi's sheet say?
qa.a: The red line said, 'Conclusion is rushed.'

qa.q: Why might the red line be all Jahnavi remembers?
qa.a: The criticism stung, so Jahnavi's attention kept going back to it, and the hurt made nine good comments fade until one line felt like the whole verdict.

qa.q: What could help Jahnavi see the whole sheet?
qa.a: Jahnavi could read the sheet again and write the nine good comments next to the one fix, then plan how to tighten the conclusion.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see the gap between the sheet and Jahnavi's story about it?
qa.a: Rafiq, who counted the ticks, seems puzzled and a bit concerned that a strong project had become 'a disaster' by evening.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager who got nine praises and one criticism and by evening remembers only the criticism.

passage:
Saturday: At the inter-school science fair, the judge spent ten minutes at Abhinav's solar dryer. 'Clever design. Good data. Very neat poster. Your costing is a little vague, though.' She moved on.
Sunday: Abhinav replayed only one sentence. Costing is vague. Costing is vague. He told Irfan on the phone, 'She basically said the whole thing was vague.' Irfan said, 'Didn't she say clever?' 'Just being polite.'
Wednesday: The score sheet came to school. Irfan read it out in the corridor: design 9, data 9, presentation 8, costing 5. 'That's your one weak spot. Everything else is top.' Abhinav took the sheet and looked at the numbers for a long time. Then he drew a small circle around the 5 and wrote next to it: ask Papa about prices.

qa.q: What score did Abhinav get for costing?
qa.a: Abhinav got 5 for costing.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav dismiss 'clever' as 'just being polite'?
qa.a: The criticism hurt, so it held Abhinav's attention, and the praise felt less believable beside it; the painful line seemed like the judge's real opinion.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Hearing all the scores read out put the 5 next to three high marks, so Abhinav could see one weak spot and plan a fix instead of feeling the whole project had failed.

qa.q: What might Irfan feel reading the score sheet aloud?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt relieved and eager to show the full picture, since the numbers proved what Irfan had been trying to say on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a teenager who hears praise and one criticism from a judge and replays only the criticism until the full score sheet is read out.

passage: Rehana, you've been staring at that one comment on your essay for an hour. Let me tell you about your Jyoti Masi at fifteen. I wrote a story for the school magazine, and the editor, a senior girl, sent it back covered in notes. 'Beautiful opening.' 'This line made me cry.' 'Great dialogue.' I think there were ten good notes. And one: 'The ending feels weak.' Guess which one I remembered? For a month I told everyone the story was weak. I nearly withdrew it. My mother made me sit and read the whole page out loud, every note, slowly. By the end I was embarrassed at how much I'd skipped. I fixed the ending in one evening. The story was printed. So, before you decide your essay is bad, read me every comment. All of them.

qa.q: What did the one criticism say about Jyoti's story?
qa.a: It said, 'The ending feels weak.'

qa.q: Why did Jyoti remember only the comment about the ending?
qa.a: The one criticism hurt, and hurt grabs attention, so the ten good notes faded and Jyoti came to see the whole story as weak.

qa.q: What turning point does Jyoti's story offer Rehana?
qa.a: Reading every comment aloud, slowly, showed how much had been skipped; Rehana can do the same with the essay before deciding it is bad.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel hearing that Masi nearly withdrew a story over one comment?
qa.a: Rehana may feel understood and a little lighter, seeing that even a grown-up once let one line outweigh ten, and may be willing to read every comment.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how, at fifteen, one criticism among ten praises was all she could remember, until the whole page was read aloud.

passage:
The power had been out since six, so Tanuja read her science project feedback by the light of her phone, which was at eight percent.

Zeenat Ma'am had written ten comments down the side of the water-filter report. "Excellent diagram." "Clear method." "Good use of local materials." "Neat tables." "Creative idea." Tanuja counted nine ticks like that. And at the bottom: "Your conclusion doesn't match your data. Please check."

The phone died.

In the dark, one line kept playing in her head: doesn't match your data. Doesn't match. She pictured Ma'am frowning as she wrote it. Ma'am must think I'm careless. The whole project is wrong.

The next morning, when her friend asked how the feedback was, Tanuja said, "Bad. Ma'am said my conclusion was wrong."

"Just that?"

Tanuja tried to remember the rest. She honestly couldn't. Something about a diagram, maybe.

qa.q: What did Zeenat Ma'am write at the bottom of the report?
qa.a: "Your conclusion doesn't match your data. Please check."

qa.q: Why can Tanuja remember only the criticism the next morning?
qa.a: The one line hurt, so her mind replayed it in the dark until it filled everything. The nine praises were dimmed because they didn't sting.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do to see the feedback more fairly?
qa.a: Reread the whole sheet in daylight and write the good comments and the one criticism side by side. Then she can fix the conclusion while remembering what she did well.

qa.q: If you were Zeenat Ma'am, how would you want Tanuja to read your comments?
qa.a: Ma'am would probably want Tanuja to feel proud of the nine good points and see the conclusion as one thing to fix. Ma'am likely didn't mean the project was wrong.

grounding: A teenage girl receives nine praises and one criticism on a project and can recall only the criticism, as the spotlight lands on what hurt.

passage:
After the school's annual day in Kolkata, Jeevan sir called Anirban to the music room. He had a feedback card for every soloist.

"Beautiful tone," he read aloud. "Great breath control. Good stage presence. You held the high note well. Your Bengali pronunciation was clear. Good eye contact. Confident entry. You listened to the tabla. You chose the right song." He paused. "The ending was a bit rushed. Slow it down next time."

Anirban said thank you and left.

That evening, when his mother asked how it went, he said, "Sir said I rushed the ending."

"What else?"

"Nothing much. Just that I rushed it." He went to his room and played the recording, skipping straight to the last thirty seconds, again and again. Each time, it sounded worse.

The card lay on his desk, face down.

qa.q: What did Jeevan sir say about the ending?
qa.a: "The ending was a bit rushed. Slow it down next time."

qa.q: Why does Anirban keep replaying only the last thirty seconds?
qa.a: The one criticism hurt, so his attention locks onto it and the nine praises fade. Replaying it makes the flaw feel bigger each time.

qa.q: What small step would help Anirban balance what he heard?
qa.a: Turn the card over and read every line aloud, maybe to his mother, then practise the ending slowly. That keeps the useful criticism without losing the praise.

qa.q: How might Jeevan sir feel if he heard Anirban say "Nothing much" about the feedback?
qa.a: Jeevan sir would probably be surprised and a little sad, having given nine real compliments. He meant the ending as a small tip, not the main message.

grounding: A teenager given nine praises and one criticism after a performance can only recall the criticism, as his mind's spotlight lands on what hurt.
